answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: Claude writes a JavaScript orchestration script (invoked with `ultracode` or a plain 'use a workflow' request) that discovers the handler files, fans out one `agent()` per file through `pipeline()`, then runs an adversarial verification phase over the findings. Once the run is right, press `s` in `/workflows` to save the script into `.claude/workflows/` so next quarter it reruns as a single project slash command.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents fanned out turn by turn by the main agent. Rejected because 400 delegations plus a verify pass outgrow what one conversation can coordinate, every intermediate finding would land in the main context window, and nothing about the orchestration itself would be repeatable next quarter.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: the workflow runtime executes the script deterministically, so the per-file fan-out, the verification stage and the concurrency caps are code, not model judgment. The model only authors the script and supplies the audit reasoning inside each spawned agent.
answers.context_boundary: The script runs in an isolated runtime separate from the conversation, and each spawned agent gets its own context window. Per-file audit results live in script variables; only the value the script returns (the verified finding list) crosses into the main session's context.
answers.lifecycle: It runs when the saved command is invoked, or when the keyword or a natural-language workflow request appears in a prompt you typed yourself. It runs in the background until the script returns, you stop it with `x`, or a runtime cap trips; it is resumable only inside the same session, and exiting Claude Code makes the next session start it fresh.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on substance: the script guarantees every file gets an auditor, but whether an auth gap is actually spotted is still model judgment, and a missed finding is silent. Operationally, there is no mid-run user input, shell or MCP calls outside your allowlist can stall a long run on a permission prompt, and stopping mid fan-out reruns every agent that started after the first unfinished one.
answers.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows need Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (on Pro you must switch on the Dynamic workflows row in `/config`); an org can kill them with `disableWorkflows` in managed settings or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1`. Watch the caps and the size guideline: 16 concurrent agents and 1,000 agents per run, and `workflowSizeGuideline` defaults to `medium` (under 15 agents) from v2.1.219, which will undersize a 400-file pass unless you set `large` or `unrestricted`.

answers.primary: An agent team: the main session becomes the lead and spawns five teammates, each given one hypothesis in its spawn prompt, with an explicit instruction to message each other and try to disprove each other's theories. They coordinate through the shared task list and their mailboxes, and the surviving consensus is written to a findings doc on disk that the lead maintains.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents. Rejected because subagents only report back to the agent that spawned them and can never talk to each other, so the adversarial cross-examination that is the whole point here is structurally impossible.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides who to spawn, what to assign, when the debate has converged and what goes in the findings doc; the harness only supplies the mailbox files, the file-locked shared task list and the optional `TeammateIdle` / `TaskCompleted` hooks (exit code 2) that can push a teammate to keep working.
answers.context_boundary: Each teammate is a full independent Claude Code session with its own context window, loading CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills from project and user settings but not the lead's conversation history. What crosses is the spawn prompt, direct `SendMessage` traffic between agents, shared task state, idle notifications, and the findings doc itself as a durable on-disk artifact.
answers.lifecycle: The team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate (you approve the spawn), and teammates run until they are asked to shut down, stopped with `x`, or the lead's session exits. The team config directory is removed at session end while the task list persists; `/resume` and `/rewind` do not restore in-process teammates, so a resumed session has to respawn them.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Nothing enforces that a hypothesis is genuinely falsified, so the team can converge on a consensus that is merely the loudest theory; teammates sometimes stop on API errors or fail to mark tasks complete, which blocks dependent tasks, and the lead often declares the investigation finished before the work is done. Token cost scales linearly with teammate count.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default: you must set `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` in settings.json or the environment, otherwise no team is set up and Claude will not spawn teammates. The documented behaviour is as of v2.1.178 (the old `TeamCreate` / `TeamDelete` tools no longer exist and `team_name` is deprecated); before v2.1.207 one malformed mailbox entry blocked delivery for that agent entirely.

answers.primary: A subagent: a test-runner subagent definition with a narrow tool allowlist (shell plus read) and a cheap model, whose system prompt says to run the suite and return only failing test names with their error messages. The main agent delegates the run to it, either by description match or by an explicit 'use the test-runner subagent' instruction.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill (or slash command) that tells Claude to run the suite and report only failures. Rejected because a skill is instructions the main agent follows in the main conversation, so the tens of thousands of raw lines enter the working context window before any filtering happens, which is exactly the outcome being ruled out.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, and this is the point of the choice: the harness owns the boundary, because a subagent genuinely runs in a separate context window and only its final message returns. The model owns what it selects to put in that final message, and the model also owns the decision to delegate at all unless a hook forces it.
answers.context_boundary: The raw suite output lives only in the subagent's own context window; the summary string it returns is the only thing that crosses into the main conversation. The subagent starts fresh with no main-session history (unless it is a forked subagent started with `/subtask`, which inherits the conversation instead).
answers.lifecycle: It runs when the main agent delegates the task, and it ends when it returns its result. Run in the background it keeps going while the session continues and shows up in `/tasks` and the @-mention typeahead; it stops applying the moment the result is returned, and it has no standing effect on later turns.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on volume. The subagent decides how much detail to return, so a verbose return can still paste a wall of output back, and a very large run can overflow the subagent's own context and lose failures to truncation. Delegation itself is advisory: nothing stops the main agent from just running the suite inline, so a PreToolUse hook that blocks the raw test command in the main session is the only hard guarantee.
answers.version_caveat: Subagents are generally available with no flag or plan gate; definitions resolve from project, user, plugin or CLI-defined scope. Note that as of v2.1.198 `/agents` no longer opens a management panel and just prints where the definition files live, so create or edit them by asking Claude or editing the files directly; a teammate inside an agent team also cannot launch a background subagent.

answers.primary: An agent team with three teammates, one per layer (frontend, backend API, tests), each given its own file ownership in the spawn prompt. They keep each other current on the evolving interface contract through direct teammate-to-teammate messaging and the shared task list, and you attach to any one of them from the agent panel (arrow keys, Enter) to redirect it without going through the lead.
answers.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow. Rejected because a workflow moves the plan into a script that admits no mid-run user input and gives you nothing to attach to, so an interface contract that changes during the work cannot be renegotiated between workers or steered by you mid-flight.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead assigns and supervises, and each teammate decides what to tell the others; the harness only provides the mailbox, the file-locked task list, the attach-and-message panel, and hooks like `TaskCompleted` if you want a gate on work being marked done.
answers.context_boundary: Three independent context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills fresh and does not inherit the lead's history, so the contract has to travel explicitly: in the spawn prompt, in messages, in the shared task list, and in the code on disk. While you are viewing a teammate, your typed text and skills go to that teammate but built-in slash commands still execute in the lead's session.
answers.lifecycle: The team exists from the first spawn until the teammates shut down or the lead's session ends; the team config directory is cleaned up automatically at session exit while the task list persists. A resumed session does not get its in-process teammates back, so a multi-day feature has to respawn them.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. Agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so any overlap in file ownership silently overwrites work; contract drift is only as good as the messages the teammates choose to send, and a teammate can code against a stale contract for a long time before anyone notices. Teammate permission prompts bubble up to the lead, so an unattended lead leaves workers stalled.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and off unless `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` is set. Display defaults to in-process from v2.1.179 (before that it was `auto`); split panes need tmux or iTerm2 with the `it2` CLI and are not supported in the VS Code integrated terminal, Windows Terminal or Ghostty. Teammates do not inherit the lead's `/model` unless you set the default teammate model in `/config`, and their model is fixed at spawn.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: Claude writes a script whose loop runs the strict type check, spawns agents to fix the reported errors, and re-runs the check, with the termination condition (passes, or two consecutive rounds with no progress) expressed in JavaScript. Save it afterwards so the same loop is a reusable command.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that instructs Claude to run the check, fix, and repeat. Rejected because then the loop and the stop rule are re-decided by the model every round, the whole transcript of every round accumulates in one context window, and 'no progress twice in a row' becomes a judgement call rather than a comparison of two counts.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime executes the loop and evaluates the stopping condition deterministically in script code, which is what removes the babysitting; the model owns only the per-round fixes inside each spawned agent.
answers.context_boundary: The script executes in an isolated workflow runtime outside the conversation. Each round's raw type-check output and fix log stay in script variables and in the agents' own contexts; only the final result (passed, or stalled after N rounds) crosses back into the session.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by invoking the workflow (saved command, or the keyword in a prompt you typed). It runs in the background while the session stays responsive and ends when the script's own condition is satisfied, when you press `x`, or when a runtime cap trips. Resume works only within the same session.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on iteration (the 1,000-agent cap makes an infinite loop impossible) but fails open on correctness: agents can make the check pass by weakening types or adding escape hatches, and the no-progress heuristic can halt with real errors outstanding. There is no mid-run input, so the only correction available is stopping the run.
answers.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (Pro users must enable Dynamic workflows in `/config`). Note the permission behaviour: workflow subagents always run in `acceptEdits` and auto-approve file edits regardless of your session's permission mode, but shell commands outside your allowlist still prompt, so allowlist the type-check command up front or the unattended loop will sit waiting on you.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: the script discovers the component files, then uses `pipeline()` to run one migration agent per file in its own isolated checkout (a worktree), followed by a verification step per file before the result counts as done. Saving the script makes the migration repeatable and inspectable.
answers.rejected_alternative: The `/batch` skill, which is the packaged subagent-plus-worktree pattern that splits a change into roughly 5 to 30 worktree-isolated subagents each opening a pull request. Rejected because 500 files far exceeds that fan-out, the per-file verification gate is not part of that pattern, and a pull request per slice is the wrong output shape here.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime owns the fan-out, the isolation of each unit of work, and the fact that a verify agent runs after each transform; the model owns the transform itself and the verdict each verifier reaches.
answers.context_boundary: The orchestration runs in the workflow runtime, separate from the conversation. Each file's agent has its own context window and its own checkout, so the file contents and diffs never enter the main session; only the aggregated result of the run crosses back.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on invocation, runs in the background, ends when the script returns or you stop it. If you stop mid fan-out, only agents that finished before the first unfinished one return from cache; every agent that started after it reruns, which is why a many-small-agents shape preserves more progress than a few long ones.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. 'Verified' is a model verdict per file, not a test run, so a subtly wrong migration can be marked done; and because each file is transformed in an isolated copy, the real risk is the merge back, where cross-file conventions and shared theme files drift out of sync. Unallowlisted shell commands can also stall a very long run on a prompt.
answers.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (Pro enables it in `/config`). Runtime caps apply: at most 16 concurrent agents (fewer on machines with limited CPU cores) and 1,000 agents total per run, which 500 files plus 500 verifiers essentially exhausts, so plan on slicing by directory. Also raise `workflowSizeGuideline` (v2.1.202 or later, default `medium` from v2.1.219) or Claude will aim far too small.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: one `agent()` per changed file through `pipeline()` for the correctness review, then a single synthesis agent that receives all per-file findings and returns one deduplicated, ranked summary. Save it as a command so the same review runs on every branch.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Rejected because inter-agent messaging and a shared task list are the entire cost of a team and this task explicitly needs none of it, and 60 teammates is an order of magnitude past the 3 to 5 range where teams stay manageable.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The script guarantees each changed file gets exactly one reviewer and that exactly one merge step runs over the complete finding set; the model owns the review content and the ranking judgement.
answers.context_boundary: Runs in the workflow runtime. Each reviewer sees only its own file in its own context, the per-file findings accumulate in script variables rather than in your session, and they are handed to the merge agent as script data. Only the final ranked summary enters the conversation's context window.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when the workflow command is invoked against the pull request, in the background, ending when the summary is returned. It applies only to that run; nothing persists between runs except the saved script itself.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open, with a specific blind spot: a reviewer that sees one file in isolation cannot see cross-file or interface-level defects, so the class of bug a 60-file pull request most often contains is the class this shape misses. The dedupe step is also a single model pass that can quietly drop a genuine finding while collapsing near-duplicates.
answers.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan; Pro users enable it in `/config`, and an organisation can disable it via managed settings. If you want this to fire on every pull request without a human invoking it, that is a different surface (GitHub Actions or GitHub code review), not a workflow gate. In `claude -p` and the Agent SDK there is no launch approval prompt, so the run starts immediately.

answers.primary: Subagents invoked in sequence from a single session: a performance-analysis subagent, then a fix subagent, then a verification subagent, with the main agent passing each one's returned result into the next one's prompt. Package the ordering as a skill or slash command so the sequence is stated once and reused.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Rejected because teammates are concurrent peers with no worktree isolation, and three of them working the same handful of hot files would overwrite each other; the documented guidance is that sequential work, same-file edits and dependency-heavy chains belong in a single session with subagents rather than a team.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. Nothing in the harness makes step two wait for step one or forces step three to happen at all; the main agent chooses the order. The harness only enforces each subagent's tool allowlist and context isolation, and hooks (PostToolUse or Stop) are the only way to make a missing verification step actually block.
answers.context_boundary: Each specialist runs in its own context window and returns only a summary, which becomes the next specialist's input. The exploration behind the performance findings never reaches the fixer, and the fixer's raw diff reasoning never reaches the verifier; the shared files on disk are the other channel between them.
answers.lifecycle: The chain starts when you make the request or run the command, each subagent ends when it returns, and the sequence is over once the verifier reports. It has no standing effect afterwards, and each rerun re-derives everything from scratch.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. The main agent can skip the verifier, re-analyse instead of consuming what it was handed, or fix things that were never on the analyser's list, and the summary-only handoff is lossy, so exact file and line detail the fixer needs can be dropped. If the strict ordering genuinely has to be guaranteed, that is the argument for moving these three steps into a workflow script.
answers.version_caveat: Subagents are generally available with no flag, plan gate or experimental status; definitions load from project, user, plugin or CLI-defined scope. `/agents` stopped opening a panel in v2.1.198 and now just points at the definition files. If the lossy handoff hurts, a forked subagent started with `/subtask` inherits the full conversation instead of starting fresh.

answers.primary: An agent team: ask the lead to spawn three teammates, one on user experience, one on technical architecture, one as devil's advocate, and to have them message each other as their arguments form. You attach to any explorer from the agent panel (arrow keys to select, Enter to open its transcript and type to it) and redirect it directly, or press Escape to interrupt its current turn.
answers.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow. A workflow can draft a plan from several independent angles and weigh them against each other, but its runtime forbids mid-run user input and there is no individual agent to attach to, so 'jump into one explorer and redirect it' is exactly what it cannot do.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides the split, the spawn prompts and when to synthesise; each teammate decides what it says to the others and whether it actually engages with the counter-arguments. The harness contributes the mailbox, the task list, the attach-and-message panel and interrupt keys.
answers.context_boundary: Three independent full sessions plus the lead, each loading CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills but none of the lead's history. What crosses is the spawn prompt, teammate-to-teammate messages, your typed redirections while attached, idle notifications back to the lead, and any design document they write to disk. While viewing a teammate, plain text and skills go to it while built-in commands still run in the lead.
answers.lifecycle: Begins when you approve the spawn, runs until the explorers are asked to shut down or the session ends. Idle teammate rows hide from the panel after about 30 seconds but the teammate is still running and addressable by name; the team directory is cleaned up on session exit.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. The devil's advocate role is only a prompt, so it can drift into agreement; the lead may synthesise before the perspectives have actually collided; and unless you explicitly ask for a written artifact the whole exploration evaporates with the session. Cost is roughly three independent sessions plus coordination overhead.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental, disabled unless `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` is set. Panel behaviour is version sensitive: idle rows are not hidden before v2.1.181, hide per-teammate in v2.1.181 through v2.1.198, and only hide once the whole panel is idle from v2.1.199 (which also warns that `/model` typed at a teammate applies to the lead). Split-pane display needs tmux or iTerm2 with `it2` (explicit `iterm2` mode from v2.1.186).

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: a review phase produces the findings, then `pipeline()` spawns one independent verifier `agent()` per finding, and the script returns a single merged summary of what survived. This is the same adversarial cross-check pattern the bundled `/deep-research` workflow uses, so ask for it as a workflow and save the script once the shape is right.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents, one verifier per finding. Rejected because a subagent reports its result back into the conversation that spawned it, so 5 to 10 verifier returns would land in the working context window one after another, which is precisely the per-finding chatter to be kept out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime guarantees that every finding gets its own verifier and that intermediate verdicts stay in script variables rather than in a context window; the model owns whether each claim actually holds up.
answers.context_boundary: The orchestration runs in an isolated runtime outside the conversation. Each verifier has its own context and sees only its finding, the verdicts accumulate as script state, and exactly one value, the final verified summary, crosses back into the session.
answers.lifecycle: Runs on invocation of the workflow, in the background while the session stays responsive, and ends when the summary is returned. Progress is visible in `/workflows` if you want it, but it is not pushed into the transcript; saving the script makes the review repeatable per branch.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open, and in a specific way: verification is model checking model, and when a verifier cannot check a claim (rate limit, API error) the claim is reported as unverified rather than refuted, so unchecked material still reaches your summary looking much like verified material. It is worth reading the unverified bucket rather than trusting the headline.
answers.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (Pro enables Dynamic workflows in `/config`); organisations can disable them entirely. The treatment of uncheckable claims as unverified rather than refuted is v2.1.196 or later, so on earlier versions genuine findings could be dropped. At 5 to 10 agents the run sits below the 25-agent large-workflow warning but may exceed a `small` size guideline.
